title: Water passes light like air, so a pool has no bottom
question: I am exploring aquatic life, and this is the gap everything else sits on: there is no depth in the water. A pool forty rows deep is the same blue at the floor as at the surface, because only rock and plants block light -- water is as clear as air to the light field. Nothing living down there could have a reason to rise toward the light, and a lake can never have a dark bottom. Is a pool that goes dark with depth what you want, and roughly how dark at forty rows?
context_md:
The engine already does this for foliage, with the right equation. `FieldTile::transmission` is **Beer-Lambert**: it counts opaque cells down each column and reads transmission off a table. That is the same law that gives a real lake its depth limit. Water is simply not counted as opaque, so it contributes nothing.

**The third image is the control**, and it is why the second one is a finding rather than a broken overlay: a cave inside rock reads pitch black on the same channel, same settings. Light does stop when something stops it.
